Watching him in these moods, I often found myself considering the old theory that the soul has two parts. I enjoyed imagining two Dupins: one who invented, and one who worked things out.

Do not take what I have just said to mean that I am describing something supernatural or writing an extravagant tale. What I noticed in the Frenchman was simply the effect of an unusually active mind, or perhaps an unhealthy one. An example will best show the kind of remarks he made at such times.

One night we were walking along a long, dirty street near the Palais Royal. Both of us seemed lost in thought, and neither had spoken a word for at least fifteen minutes. Suddenly Dupin said:

“He is certainly a very small fellow, and he would do better at the Théâtre des Variétés.”

“There's no doubt about that,” I answered without thinking. I was so absorbed in my thoughts that I did not immediately notice how extraordinarily his words had matched them. A moment later I came to myself, deeply astonished.

“Dupin,” I said seriously, “this is beyond anything I can understand. I freely admit I'm amazed. I can hardly trust my senses. How could you possibly know I was thinking about ——?” I stopped there, to make quite certain he really knew who was in my mind.

“—— Chantilly,” he said. “Why stop? You were telling yourself that his tiny frame made him unsuitable for tragedy.”

That was exactly what I had been thinking. Chantilly had formerly worked as a shoemaker in the Rue St. Denis. Becoming obsessed with the stage, he had tried to play Xerxes in Crébillon's tragedy of that name, and had been publicly and mercilessly mocked for his efforts.

“For heaven's sake, tell me,” I cried, “what method—if there is a method—has allowed you to read so deeply into my mind.” In truth, I was even more shaken than I wanted to admit.

“It was the fruit seller,” my friend replied, “who led you to decide that the man who mended soles was too short to play Xerxes and others of that sort.”

“The fruit seller! You astonish me. I don't know any fruit seller at all.”

“The man who bumped into you as we entered this street, perhaps fifteen minutes ago.”

I now remembered that a fruit seller carrying a large basket of apples on his head had indeed almost knocked me over by accident. It happened as we turned from the Rue C—— into the street where we now stood. But I could not possibly understand what that had to do with Chantilly.

The painter suddenly appeared in the studio doorway, beckoning them in with sharp, impatient gestures. They glanced at one another and smiled.

“I'm waiting,” he called. “Please come inside. The light is absolutely perfect, and you can bring your drinks.”

They got up and strolled together down the path. Two butterflies, green and white, fluttered past, and a thrush began singing in the pear tree at the garden's corner.

“You're glad you've met me, Mr. Gray,” Lord Henry said, looking at him.

“Yes, I'm glad now. I wonder whether I'll always be glad.”

“Always! What a dreadful word. Hearing it makes me shudder. Women are so fond of saying it. They ruin every romance by trying to make it last forever. And the word means nothing. The only difference between a passing fancy and a lifelong passion is that the passing fancy lasts a little longer.”

Entering the studio, Dorian Gray rested his hand on Lord Henry's arm. “Then let our friendship be a passing fancy,” he murmured, blushing at his own boldness. He stepped onto the platform and took up his pose again.

Lord Henry dropped into a large wicker armchair and watched him. Only the sweep and flick of the brush across the canvas disturbed the silence, apart from Hallward's occasional steps backward to examine his work at a distance. Dust danced gold in the slanting shafts of light coming through the open door. The rich fragrance of roses seemed to hang over everything.

About fifteen minutes later, Hallward put down his work. He studied Dorian Gray for a long time, then studied the painting just as long, frowning and biting the end of one of his enormous brushes. “It's completely finished,” he announced at last. Bending down, he signed his name in long vermilion letters in the canvas's left-hand corner.

Lord Henry walked over to inspect the painting. It was unquestionably a remarkable work of art, and a remarkable likeness too.

“My dear fellow, you have my warmest congratulations,” he said. “It's the finest portrait of our time. Mr. Gray, come and see yourself.”

The young man gave a start, as though waking from a dream.

“Is it really finished?” he murmured as he stepped off the platform.

“Entirely finished,” the painter replied. “And you've been a splendid sitter today. I'm tremendously grateful to you.”

“You have me to thank for that,” Lord Henry interrupted. “Haven't you, Mr. Gray?”

Dorian said nothing. He drifted listlessly into position before his portrait and turned to face it.

When we got back to the raft, he counted his money and found he'd collected eighty-seven dollars and seventy-five cents. He'd also brought along a three-gallon jug of whisky he'd found under a wagon as he started home through the woods. The king said, all things considered, it beat every day he'd ever spent in the missionary business. There was no arguing about it, he said: heathens weren't worth a thing compared with pirates when you were working a religious camp meeting.

The duke had thought he'd done pretty well himself, until the king turned up. After that he wasn't nearly so pleased. At the printing office he'd set up and printed two small jobs for farmers, advertisements for horses, and collected four dollars. He'd also brought in ten dollars' worth of newspaper advertisements, offering to print them for four dollars if the customers paid in advance. So they did. The newspaper cost two dollars a year, but he sold three subscriptions for fifty cents each, provided they paid him straightaway. They'd expected to pay in firewood and onions as usual. He told them he'd just bought the business, cut the price as low as he could afford, and intended to accept cash only. He'd set up a little poem too, which he made up entirely himself: three verses, sweet and rather sad, called “Yes, crush, cold world, this breaking heart.” He left it ready to print in the newspaper and charged nothing for it. Altogether he took in nine dollars and fifty cents, and said he'd done a fair day's work to earn it.

Then he showed us another little printing job he'd done for free, because it was for us. It showed an escaped black slave carrying a bundle on a stick over his shoulder, with “$200 reward” printed underneath. The words were all about Jim and described him exactly. They said he'd run away the previous winter from St. Jacques' plantation, forty miles below New Orleans, and had probably headed north. Anyone who caught him and sent him back would receive the reward and their expenses.

“Now,” the duke said, “after tonight we can travel in daylight whenever we like. Any time we see someone coming, we can tie Jim's hands and feet with rope and put him in the wigwam. We'll show this handbill and say we caught him upriver, but we were too poor to take a steamboat. So our friends let us have this little raft on credit, and we're heading down to collect the reward.
